Service

The production pcs-service binary: TOML config, factory registry, HTTP control plane, and built-in standalone & Raft cluster runners.

Overview

The service feature ships a runnable binary plus a small framework for pointing a TOML-driven service at a pipeline and plugging in custom sources and sinks. It implies io, distributed, and tracing. Raft is not implied — use service-cluster for that.

Two top-level modes:

  • standalone — a single instance driving sources into the pipeline and sinks out of it. Good for simple deployments and testing.
  • cluster (feature = "service-cluster") — a Raft-coordinated cluster of instances sharing partition assignment and checkpoint state.

Install & build

cargo install --path crates/pcs-service --features service-cluster
# or, build from source:
cargo build --release --bin pcs-service --features service-cluster

TOML configuration

A ServiceConfig describes the mode, the node identity, where the pipeline comes from, and optional sources / sinks. The control plane ([http]) is always available.

There is no TOML path for declaring systems or components: the pipeline is a WebAssembly guest component that reports its own component schemas through the describe() export. Unknown keys are rejected rather than dropped, so a stale [[pipeline.systems]] section is a parse error. 

mode = "standalone"

[node]
id = 1
data_dir = "/var/lib/pcs/node-1"

[run_mode]
kind = "interval"
interval_ms = 5000

[pipeline.wasm]
module = "/var/lib/pcs/pipelines/trades.wasm"
# Optional integrity check; the service refuses to start on mismatch.
# sha3_256 = "abc123..."

# String key/values the guest reads through the host-io `get-config` import.
[pipeline.wasm.config]
fx_provider = "ecb_daily"

[[sources]]
name = "trades_in"
type = "ParquetSource"
target_component = "Trade"

[sources.config]
path = "/data/in/trades.parquet"

[[sinks]]
name = "trades_out"
type = "ParquetSink"
source_component = "Trade"

[sinks.config]
path = "/data/out/trades.parquet"

[http]
bind = "0.0.0.0:8080"

Plugging in your own sources and sinks

The TOML refers to sources and sinks by type name. To map a name to your own implementation, register a factory on the ServiceBuilder before calling build(). Built-in factories for Parquet, CSV, and JSON Lines come from register_builtin_factories. 

use pcs_service::service::config::ServiceConfig;
use pcs_service::service::factories::register_builtin_factories;
use pcs_service::service::{ServiceBuilder, run_standalone};
use tokio_util::sync::CancellationToken;

let config = ServiceConfig::load("service.toml")?;

let built = register_builtin_factories(ServiceBuilder::new())
    .register_source(MyKafkaSourceFactory)
    .register_sink(MyPostgresSinkFactory)
    .build(&config)?;

// The trailing `None` opts out of publishing live stats to the HTTP control plane.
let stats = run_standalone(built, &config, CancellationToken::new(), None).await?;

Each factory takes a toml::Value — the config table from the TOML — and returns a boxed Source or Sink. A binary that builds its pipeline in Rust rather than loading a component calls ServiceBuilder::with_runtime with a Box<dyn PipelineRuntime> and omits the [pipeline] table entirely.

CLI

# Single-node:
pcs-service serve --config service.toml

# Validate config without starting:
pcs-service validate --config service.toml

# Inspect a running instance:
pcs-service status --server http://localhost:8080

# Cluster lifecycle (requires service-cluster feature):
pcs-service cluster init   --config cluster.toml --node-id 1
pcs-service cluster join   --server http://leader:8081 --node-id 2
pcs-service cluster leave  --server http://leader:8081 --node-id 2
pcs-service cluster status --server http://leader:8081

HTTP control plane

EndpointReturns
GET /health200 if the process is up; cheap liveness probe.
GET /ready200 once the service has loaded config and registered factories. Use as Kubernetes readiness probe.
GET /metricsPrometheus exposition format. Pipeline durations, retry counts, claim lifecycles, Raft term/leader.
GET /statusJSON snapshot of pipeline state, last RunStats, claim ledger, current Raft membership.

Deploying a cluster

A 3-node Raft cluster is the typical production target. Start the leader with cluster init, then have followers cluster join against the leader’s control-plane URL. Each node needs:

  • A unique node_id.
  • A reachable Raft TCP listen address (default 7001).
  • Two redb files: log store + state machine. Pre-create the parent directory.

See the operations guide for full deployment steps, capacity planning, and runbooks for common failure scenarios.
